scales-of-analysis-s1.title: South Asia: income groups of countries

map.label: Shaded map of South Asia by World Bank income group: Sri Lanka is upper-middle income, Afghanistan is low income, and India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan are lower-middle income
map.legendTitle: World Bank FY27 income group (by income per person)

scales-of-analysis-s2.title: Country A: households earning above the national middle income, by province

map.label: Shaded map of Country A by province: the share of households earning above the national middle income is highest in the Capital Region and on the South Coast and lowest in the Western Uplands and Southern Forest
map.legendTitle: Households above the national middle income (percent, invented)

items.q: The map covers the region of South Asia. At what scale of analysis are its data?
options: National: each shade is one value for one country
Regional: the map covers South Asia
Global: income groups are set for the whole world
Local: India's states are shown inside it

why.correct: Read the unit of the data, not the area of the map: one value per country is the national scale.
options: Right: the unit each value describes is a country, so the data are national, even though the map shows a region.
The area shown is a region, but the scale of analysis is set by the unit of the data: countries.
The groups are worldwide categories, but each value here describes one country.
India is one shade; no states are shown.

items.q: Which statement describes the pattern at this scale, naming places?
options: India is upper-middle income, and Sri Lanka and Afghanistan are both low income
Sri Lanka upper-middle, Afghanistan low, and the other five lower-middle income
The seven countries share one income group, lower-middle income, across the map
Afghanistan and Sri Lanka are upper-middle income, India low income

why.correct: Name the places in each class from the legend.
options: India is lower-middle; Sri Lanka is upper-middle.
Right: it names each class and the places in it (World Bank FY27).
Three classes appear on the map, not one.
This swaps the classes: Afghanistan is low income and India lower-middle.

items.q: India is one shade on this map. What would a map of India's states, at the local scale, most likely show?
options: One income group in each state, matching India's single shade at the national scale
Nothing new, because local data repeat what the national data already show
Big gaps: states such as Goa far richer per person than others, such as Bihar
Data for South Asia's other countries, which this map leaves out

why.correct: A pattern at one scale can hide a different pattern at a smaller scale.
options: A national shade is an average of very different states, not a sign that they match.
Local data often show patterns that national data hide.
Right: one national value blends rich and poor states; a map of the states would reveal them.
A map of India's states would show India, not its neighbors.

items.q: A report gives one figure for Country A: half of all households earn above the middle income. What does the map add?
options: Each province has about half of its households above the middle income, like the nation
Country A earns more than its neighbors, as the national figure shows
Incomes are rising fastest in the Western Uplands and the Southern Forest
They cluster in the Capital Region and South Coast; few are in the Western Uplands

why.correct: Data at a smaller scale show variation that one national figure hides.
options: The provinces differ widely; "half" is only the national figure.
No other country is on the map.
The map shows one date, so it cannot show which incomes are rising.
Right: the provinces range from under 35% to 65% or more, so the national figure hides a gap.

items.q: The national figure was made by adding up the households of all eight provinces into one number. What is this called, and what is its drawback?
options: Aggregated data; one value for all provinces hides how they differ
Qualitative data; it is built from words, so it is hard to put on a map
Remote sensing; it was measured by satellite, so it misses people
A spatial pattern; it shows where households are clustered

why.correct: Aggregated data combine small units into a larger one. They are useful for comparing countries, but they hide variation inside.
options: Right: aggregating smaller units into a bigger one makes a single figure that can hide large differences.
The national figure is a number, so it is quantitative.
Household incomes come from surveys or a census, not satellites.
One national number cannot show where anything is clustered.

items.q: A large new port opens on the South Coast, linking it to world shipping. Which effect across scales is most likely?
options: The port changes nothing in Country A, because world trade happens at the global scale
Global trade brings jobs to the coast, so its gap with the uplands may widen
Incomes in each province rise by the same amount, because the port belongs to the nation
The Western Uplands gain the most, because they are farthest from the new port

why.correct: Processes at one scale (global trade) shape patterns at another (one province), so explain the link across scales.
options: Global processes have local effects; that is the point of linking scales.
Right: a global process (world trade) has a local effect (coastal jobs), which can change the national pattern.
Effects are uneven: places near the port gain most.
Distance decay suggests the places nearest the port gain most.

items.q: At what scale of analysis should a minister read this map to decide which provinces get new job programs?
options: National, because the minister works for the whole country
Global, because jobs depend on world trade
Local (subnational), since the choice is between provinces
Regional, because Country A is part of a world region

why.correct: Match the scale of the data to the scale of the decision.
options: The minister works nationally, but the decision is about which provinces.
World trade matters, but the choice is between Country A's provinces.
Right: a choice between provinces needs data by province.
Regional data would compare countries, not provinces.

items.q: Stack the four scales of analysis from the largest area at the top to the smallest at the bottom.

model.title: Scales of analysis, largest to smallest

slips.why: A region such as South Asia holds several countries, so it is larger than one nation.
Map scale is a ratio for drawing a map, not a scale of analysis.

why.correct: Global, regional, national, local: each fits inside the one above it.

items.q: A map of a United States presidential election colored by state shows large blocks of one color. A map of the same election by county shows cities voting differently from nearby rural counties. What does this show?
options: State maps are wrong and should not be used to report the results of an election
County maps show a different election from the one shown on the state map
Rural counties and cities vote the same way, as the state map shows
Patterns change with scale: county data show a city and rural divide that states hide

why.correct: Changing the scale of analysis can reveal patterns that larger units hide.
options: Each map is accurate for its units; they answer different questions.
It is the same election, counted in smaller units.
The county map shows cities and rural counties voting differently.
Right: the same votes, grouped by smaller units, show a different pattern.

items.q: Rising world demand for avocados led farmers in Michoacán, Mexico, to plant more avocado orchards on hillsides that were forest. Which scales does this example link?
options: A global process (world demand) and a local change (land use in Michoacán)
A national process (Mexican law) and a global change (world climate)
A local process (one farm) and a regional change (across Latin America)
A regional process (South Asian trade) and a national change (Mexico's border)

why.correct: Explaining across scales means linking a process at one scale to its effect at another.
options: Right: demand far away changes land use in one part of one country.
The example is about world demand, not a national law.
The change is in one Mexican state, driven by world demand.
South Asia is not part of the example.

items.q: A student finds that Brazil's national average rainfall is moderate and concludes that the city of Manaus gets moderate rain. Why is this conclusion weak?
options: Rainfall data are qualitative, so averaging them gives a misleading number
A national average is aggregated, so it hides very wet places like the Amazon
Manaus is outside Brazil, so Brazil's national data leave the city out
Rainfall is measured at the global scale, so national averages are wrong

why.correct: Do not apply an aggregated national value to one local place; check data at the local scale.
options: Rainfall is measured in millimeters: quantitative.
Right: an average for a huge country blends very different climates; Manaus, in the Amazon, is far wetter than the national average.
Manaus is in Brazil, in the Amazon region.
Rainfall is measured at weather stations, place by place.

items.q: Sea level is rising around the world as the oceans warm. Officials in Miami, Florida, raise streets and install pumps. How do these scales relate?
options: A local process causes a global effect, which the national government answers
A national process causes a regional effect, which the world answers
A global process has a local effect, which a local government answers
The scales are unrelated, since Miami's streets are local

why.correct: Many local problems have global causes. Name both scales and the link.
options: Miami did not cause the global rise; it is responding to it.
The process is global and the response is by a city.
Right: rising seas are global; flooded streets and the city's response are local.
The local problem comes from a global process, so the scales are linked.

items.q: Why might a national government and a city mayor reach different conclusions from the same health data?
options: One of the two is reading the data wrongly, since data give one answer
Health data are global, so neither leader can use them for a decision
Mayors use qualitative data, while national governments use quantitative data
Each reads the data at a different scale, with its own pattern

why.correct: Different scales can support different, valid conclusions, so always state your scale.
options: Both can be right; they are asking about different units.
Health data are collected locally and can be read at every scale.
Both mayors and governments use many kinds of data.
Right: a national average may look fine while one city or neighborhood has a serious problem.

items.q: A world map shows that most of the world's largest cities are in Asia. A map of Japan shows that most Japanese people live on a narrow coastal strip. Which statement uses both scales correctly?
options: At the global scale, Asia holds many large cities; at the national scale, Japan's people crowd its coasts
At the global scale, Japan's coast is crowded; at the national scale, Asia holds many large cities
Both maps are at the local scale, because both show cities on coasts
Both maps are at the global scale, because Japan is part of the world map

why.correct: Tie each pattern to the scale of the map that shows it.
options: Right: each pattern is named at the scale of its own map.
This swaps the scales: the world map compares regions, and the map of Japan shows one country.
Neither map is local: one shows the world, the other one country.
A map of one country shows a national pattern, even though the country is also on the world map.

items.q: Build a sentence that compares a pattern at two scales.

specific.frame: At the ___ scale, ___, whereas at the ___ scale, ___.
specific.model: At the national scale, Country A has half its households above the middle income, whereas at the local scale, the Capital Region is above 65% and the Western Uplands below 35%.

scaleA.label: First scale
options: national
global

why.1: The figure for all of Country A is national, not global.

patternA.label: Pattern at the first scale
options: Country A has half its households above the middle income
the map has eight provinces

why.1: That is a fact about the map, not a pattern in the data.

scaleB.label: Second scale
options: local
regional

why.1: Provinces inside one country are local, not regional.

patternB.label: Pattern at the second scale
options: the Capital Region is above 65% and the Western Uplands below 35%
incomes vary

why.1: Too vague: name the places and values.

why.correct: A compare across scales names both scales and a pattern at each, with places.
